c813fd2bc859cb5fa88341f68769b6ced88b959f.summary: A Substack blog post by Natto Team, titled Part One of a piece on Russian extortion operations and hybrid warfare. It was published 2024-05-01 and archived 2026-11-25. The excerpt holds only quotes: Vladimir Putin's 2017 remarks and hacker Pavel Sitnikov's 2020 interview on state-aligned hacking, plus a truncated question about CL0P ransomware and U.S. critical infrastructure. The post is paywalled after the excerpt, so no findings, techniques or attributions appear in this text.

c87961c73eb96062c14d4b93e03dc45bd6b7cebd.summary: Symantec (Broadcom) protection bulletin on SteganoAmor, a campaign the bulletin attributes to threat group TA558. Per the bulletin, the campaign hides malicious code inside image files (steganography) and still uses the 2017 Microsoft Office Equation Editor flaw CVE-2017-11882. The group is said to target tourism and hospitality, with extensive focus on Latin America. Delivered payloads may include Remcos, Agent Tesla, Formbook, Guloader, Lokibot and Xworm.

It uses phishing emails and custom malware including loaders, backdoors and RATs. The name was given by Positive Technologies. Compromises reportedly lasted up to ten months and over a year. The report says the group is believed to have started operating in 2017 and may also target Chinese firms for financial gain.

c88964f86dee3dddad544afaa958f19d5b078700.summary: Cybereason reports on targeted attacks against Japanese companies that used the ONI ransomware and a DiskCryptor-based bootkit, MBR-ONI, which it says come from the same threat actor. Attacks began with spear-phishing that dropped the Ammyy Admin RAT, moved laterally to domain controllers, wiped more than 460 event logs, and deployed ONI through Group Policy. The attacks lasted three to nine months. The report suspects ONI and MBR-ONI were used as wipers to hide the operation, though it classes MBR-ONI as ransomware on technical grounds.

c8939694e238bdf6f51ada44d90f0e4018836ef3.summary: CUJO AI's March 2021 analysis of the Linux version of the Prometei botnet, which first appeared in December 2020. Prometei was originally a modular Windows botnet that mined Monero. The Linux sample installs itself with root or user-level privileges, sets up persistence through a system service and a cron job, and checks in to a command server. Its commands include starting a Monero miner (XMRig) and routing traffic through Tor or I2P proxy modules. The report calls it most likely an early development version and says it is unclear whether the Windows and Linux developers are the same group.
